title: Exact finite-valued functors on finite continuous group sets are forgetful
statement: Let $G$ be a topological group. Let $\mathcal C_G$ be the category whose objects are finite sets with a continuous left $G$-action (each finite set has the discrete topology), and whose morphisms are $G$-equivariant maps. Let $U:\mathcal C_G\to\mathbf{Sets}$ send an action to its underlying set. If $H:\mathcal C_G\to\mathbf{Sets}$ preserves finite limits and finite colimits, that is, is exact in the sense of [def-galois-exact-functor], and $H(S)$ is finite for every $S\in\mathcal C_G$, then there exists a natural isomorphism $U\xrightarrow{\sim}H$.

proof.text: Use the usual finite-set constructions in $\mathcal C_G$: the empty set and singleton, finite disjoint unions and products, invariant equalizer subsets and pullback subsets, and quotients by invariant equivalence relations. They have the expected universal properties because the induced maps are equivariant. These actions are continuous: stabilizers in products are finite intersections of open stabilizers; stabilizers in invariant subsets are unchanged; and the stabilizer of a quotient class contains the open stabilizer of any representative. For a discrete action, open stabilizers imply continuity since the inverse image of a point under an orbit map is a coset of a stabilizer, and each slice with a fixed second coordinate is open. Thus these particular finite limits and colimits have the usual underlying sets. By [def-galois-exact-functor], $H$ preserves all these cones and cocones; in particular $H(\emptyset)=\emptyset$ and $H(\{*\})$ is a singleton, up to their canonical identifications.

If $X$ is a nonempty finite continuous $G$-set, the pushout of $\{*\}\leftarrow X\to\{*\}$ is a singleton: in the disjoint union of the two singletons the two points are identified by any element of $X$. If $H(X)$ were empty, its image span would instead have a two-element pushout. Since $H$ preserves this pushout and the singleton, this is impossible. Hence $H(X)$ is nonempty.

For later use, let $q:A\to B$ be an equivariant surjection between finite continuous $G$-sets, and put $R=A\times_B A$. Then $q$ is the coequalizer of the two projections $R\rightrightarrows A$: a map constant on each fibre has the unique induced map on $B$, and it is equivariant by surjectivity of $q$. Exactness therefore makes $H(q)$ a coequalizer in sets, hence surjective. Indeed a set coequalizer is the quotient by the equivalence relation generated by the indicated pairs, so its quotient map is onto. This argument includes $A=B=\emptyset$. Also exactness identifies $H(R)$ with $H(A)\times_{H(B)}H(A)$, with its two projection maps.

Let $N\triangleleft G$ be open and of finite index, and write $Q_N=G/N$ with its continuous left action. Put $m=|Q_N|$ and $n=|H(Q_N)|$, both finite and positive by step 2. There is an equivariant bijection $\coprod_{a\in G/N}Q_N\to Q_N\times Q_N$, sending the point $gN$ of the $a$-summand to $(gN,gaN)$. Its inverse records the first coordinate and their quotient $g^{-1}hN$; normality makes both formulas well defined. Preserving this product and coproduct gives $n^2=mn$. Cancelling the positive integer $n$ yields $|H(Q_N)|=|Q_N|$.

Index the open normal finite-index subgroups by an arrow $M\to N$ when $M\subseteq N$, with quotient map $p_{MN}:Q_M\to Q_N$. This is a small cofiltered category: its objects form a subset of the power set of $G$, it contains $G$, any two objects have the common refinement $M\cap N$, and there are no distinct parallel arrows. Intersections remain open, normal and finite-index (the map $G/(M\cap N)\to G/M\times G/N$ is injective). The functor $N\mapsto H(Q_N)$ has finite nonempty values by the hypothesis and step 2. Apply [lem-trf-cofiltered-finite-sets-section] to choose $\gamma_N\in H(Q_N)$ for every $N$, satisfying $H(p_{MN})(\gamma_M)=\gamma_N$. Its smallness hypothesis applies because this indexing category is an actual set of subgroups; no large category of all finite actions indexes this limit.

proof.text: For a finite continuous action $X$, the subgroup $K_X=\bigcap_{x\in X}\operatorname{Stab}_G(x)$ is open (a finite intersection of open stabilizers), normal (the action kernel), and finite-index (the action embeds $G/K_X$ into the finite permutation group of $X$). If $N\subseteq K_X$ is an open normal finite-index subgroup, every $x\in X$ defines the equivariant map $f_{N,x}:Q_N\to X$, $gN\mapsto gx$. Define $t_X(x)=H(f_{N,x})(\gamma_N)$. For two choices $N,N'$, use $M=N\cap N'$: the identities $f_{M,x}=f_{N,x}p_{MN}=f_{N',x}p_{MN'}$ and compatibility of $\gamma$ show independence. For an equivariant map $a:X\to Y$, choose $N\subseteq K_X\cap K_Y$; then $a f_{N,x}=f_{N,a(x)}$, so $H(a)t_X(x)=t_Y(a(x))$. For $X=\emptyset$ use the unique empty map. Thus $t:U\to H$ is a natural transformation. This explicitly supplies the source's omitted colimit-of-Hom identification without invoking a separate representability theorem.

For $Q_N$ the map in step 6 is $t_{Q_N}(aN)=H(R_a)(\gamma_N)$, where $R_a(gN)=gaN$; here $K_{Q_N}=N$. If $aN\ne bN$, the equalizer of $R_a,R_b:Q_N\to Q_N$ is empty, since $gaN=gbN$ would imply $aN=bN$. By preservation of equalizers and of the empty set, the set equalizer of $H(R_a)$ and $H(R_b)$ is empty. In particular $H(R_a)(\gamma_N)\ne H(R_b)(\gamma_N)$. Hence $t_{Q_N}$ is injective, and the cardinality equality of step 4 makes it bijective.

Preservation of finite coproducts and naturality for their inclusions identify $t_{\coprod_i Q_{N_i}}$ with the disjoint union of the bijections $t_{Q_{N_i}}$, so it is bijective, including the empty coproduct. For any $X$, choose $N=K_X$ and the equivariant surjection $q:Y=\coprod_{x\in X}Q_N\to X$ whose $x$-summand is $f_{N,x}$. It is onto because $f_{N,x}(eN)=x$. Step 3 says $H(q)$ is onto, and $t_Y$ is bijective. Given $z\in H(X)$, choose $v\in H(Y)$ with $H(q)(v)=z$ and $y\in Y$ with $t_Y(y)=v$. Naturality gives $t_X(q(y))=z$. Thus $t_X$ is surjective for every finite action $X$.

Use $q:Y\to X$ from step 8 and $R=Y\times_XY$. Suppose $t_X(x)=t_X(x')$; choose $y,y'\in Y$ over $x,x'$. Naturality implies $H(q)(t_Y(y))=H(q)(t_Y(y'))$. The pullback identification of step 3 supplies $r_H\in H(R)$ with projections $t_Y(y),t_Y(y')$. Step 8, applied to the finite continuous action $R$, supplies $r\in R$ with $t_R(r)=r_H$. Naturality for the two projections gives $t_Y(\operatorname{pr}_1r)=t_Y(y)$ and $t_Y(\operatorname{pr}_2r)=t_Y(y')$. Injectivity of $t_Y$ yields $\operatorname{pr}_1r=y$, $\operatorname{pr}_2r=y'$, and hence $x=q(y)=q(y')=x'$ by the definition of $R$. Thus all $t_X$ are bijections. Their inverse functions are natural: from $H(a)t_X=t_YU(a)$, composing with these inverses gives $U(a)t_X^{-1}=t_Y^{-1}H(a)$. Therefore $t$ is the required natural isomorphism $U\xrightarrow{\sim}H$.
